sections.title: Cheatfile structure
intro: Name the file after the game's Title ID, for example `PCSH00297.psv`, and place it in `ux0:vitacheat/db/`. Check the Title ID and version in `sce_sys/param.sfo`.
A file contains game information, entry names, and code lines. Consecutive code lines under one entry form a single cheat.
fields: Include the Title ID, game name, and version.
This is the original VitaCheat file meaning.
Overlay reads the flag but never automatically enables it in a new session.
Followed by the operation, address, and value fields.
notes: Z06 uses UTF-8. The old manual's ANSI requirement belongs to Z04. Overlay supports UTF-8 and GBK.
Example addresses explain the format; they are not universal cheats. The Title ID, game version, and actual memory layout must match.

examples.title: Example file
examples.text: Start each entry with `_V0` or `_V1`. The following `$` lines belong to that entry.

sections.title: Anatomy of a code line
intro: Separate the three hexadecimal fields with spaces. `AAAA` has four digits; the other fields have eight each. Pad them even when writing only one byte.
The opcode determines what each field means. A copy uses the third field as a source address; a compressed write uses a parameter line for count and strides.
fields: Code family, width, controlled line count, or pointer depth.
Usually the destination; may also be a base address, mode, or stride.
Usually the value; may also be a source address, offset, or button mask.
8 / 16 / 32 bits. A 32-bit field can also store a floating-point bit pattern.
notes: All numbers are hexadecimal. For example, `0000000A` means decimal 10.
Encode a 32-bit float as its IEEE 754 bit pattern: `1.0` is `3F800000`. A decimal string in a code is not a floating-point conversion.

examples.title: A 32-bit value
examples.text: Opcode `0200` is a direct 32-bit write. `05F5E0FF` is decimal 99,999,999.

sections.title: Direct writes
intro: Write one 8-, 16-, or 32-bit value to a data address. There is no parameter line.
fields: The valid memory address to write.
Use the low 2 hex digits for 8 bits, the low 4 for 16 bits, or all 8 for 32 bits.
notes: Turning an ordinary data entry OFF stops future writes. It does not guarantee restoration of an earlier game value.

examples.title: 32-bit write
examples.text: Write the 32-bit encoding of decimal 99,999,999 at the destination.

sections.title: Memory copies
intro: Read a value from the source and write it to the destination. The third field is an address, not a literal value.

examples.title: 16-bit copy
examples.text: Read 16 bits at `0x821F4FB6` and copy them to `0x821F4FB8`.

sections.title: Compressed writes
intro: Express repeated writes in two lines. The first supplies the initial address and value; the second supplies the count and both strides. Do not interpret the parameter line as an independent opcode.
fields: The first write uses these values.
The difference between consecutive destinations, in bytes.
The increment after each write; 0 keeps the same value.

examples.title: Four consecutive writes
examples.text: Write four 16-bit values. Increase the address by 6 and the value by 1 each time.

sections.title: Pointer writes
intro: Read a pointer at the base, add an offset, and repeat at each level. The final destination depends on the pointer values; it is not the sum of all offsets added to the base.
fields: The number of pointer lines, excluding the final `3300` line.
Where the first pointer is read.
Add each offset after reading that level's pointer.
The second field is 0; the third is the value to write.

examples.title: A three-level pointer
examples.text: Read through the chain with offsets `EA20`, `100`, and `C4`, then write decimal 99,999 as a 32-bit value.

sections.title: Pointer copies
intro: Resolve separate destination and source pointer chains, then copy the value between their final addresses. End the two chains with `8800` and `8900`.
sections.syntax:
$8XZZ BBBBBBBB OOOOOOO1
$8X00 00000000 OOOOOOO2
…
$8800 00000000 00000000
$8YZZ DDDDDDDD PPPPPPP1
$8Y00 00000000 PPPPPPP2
…
$8900 00000000 00000000
fields: Each chain supplies its depth and offsets.
The second and third fields are both 0.
The second and third fields are both 0.
notes: The Z04 manual requires equal depths and widths for both chains. This example follows that rule; do not assume an older restriction defines every later implementation's capabilities.

examples.title: Three-level, 16-bit pointer copy
examples.text: The destination offsets are `47E80 → 4 → 2E8`; the source offsets are `10 → 14 → 2EC`. Copy the final 16-bit value.

sections.title: Compressed pointer writes
intro: Combine a pointer chain with repeated writes. Repetition can change the base, an intermediate level, or the final level; it does not always change only the final destination.
sections.syntax:
$7XYY BBBBBBBB OOOOOOO1
$7X00 00000000 OOOOOOO2
…
$77ZZ 00000000 CCCCCCCC
$NNNN SSSSSSSS VVVVVVVV
fields: The number of pointer lines, excluding `77ZZ` and the parameter line.
`0 ≤ ZZ ≤ YY`: 0 advances the base; YY advances the last level.
Its width is selected by X in the first line.
Advance the selected level and increment the write value.

examples.title: Repeat at the final level
examples.text: A three-level chain with `ZZ=3`. The last offset is `8`, `10`, `18`, then `20` (hexadecimal). Write the same 32-bit value each time.

examples.title: Repeat at the first level
examples.text: A three-level chain with `ZZ=1`. The first offset is `10100`, `10104`, `10108`, `1010C`, then `10110`. Write 8-bit values `60` through `64`, resolving the remaining chain again each time.

examples.title: Repeat at the base
examples.text: With `ZZ=0`, the bases are `82E40F10`, `82E40F20`, `82E40F30`, `82E40F40`, `82E40F50`, and `82E40F60`. Follow the four-level chain and write 16-bit `270F` each time.

sections.title: Instruction writes
intro: Patch instructions in the text segment. The manual defines 16- and 32-bit writes; choose the address and length for the actual ARM or Thumb instruction boundary.
fields: Use the low 4 hex digits for 16 bits or all 8 for 32 bits.
notes: ARM / Thumb storage here is little-endian. Supply the numeric bit pattern; do not reverse the number again.
Turning an A patch OFF releases it and restores its saved original bytes. B2 changes the address basis; it is not the restoration mechanism.
This section retains A100 / A200 as listed in the manual. Consult the relevant project version for additional subtypes.

examples.title: 16-bit Thumb NOP
examples.text: Write halfword `BF00`; its bytes in memory are `00 BF`. This example is a Thumb NOP.

examples.title: 32-bit instruction pattern
examples.text: Write numeric value `BE12F075`; the memory bytes are `75 F0 12 BE`. Interpret the instruction using the actual instruction set and address.

sections.title: Module-relative addressing
intro: Z06 extends B2 to select a module index and segment. Relative addresses in following codes use that segment's current base, reducing dependence on a fixed load address.
fields: The hexadecimal index in the low two opcode digits. It is not a module UID.
notes: Original Z06 dumps record module information in a matching `.txt` file. Dynamic loading/unloading can change indexes; an index is not a stable module identity.
A module base provides relative positioning, not a guarantee of equal offsets or instructions across different game versions.

examples.title: Module 0, text-segment patch
examples.text: Write a 16-bit patch at module 0's seg0 base plus `001CD8C4`.

examples.title: Module 0, repeated data writes
examples.text: Select seg1, start at relative offset `00FFF96C`, and write 8-bit `63` for `6F` iterations with address stride 1.

sections.title: Button conditions
intro: The condition controls the next AA code lines. Combine button values with bitwise OR; for example, L + R is `00000300`.
fields: The hexadecimal number of following controlled code lines.
The Z04 definitions appear below. This is a version-dependent field.
Combine individual button values with bitwise OR.
notes: Z04 device modes: 0 no match, 1 Vita, 2 PSTV, 4 DualShock 3, and 8 DualShock 4.
Z06 / Overlay compare the complete button mask and do not identify the controller through the device field. Holding another button in addition to L + R is not the same combination.
Count physical code lines, including multiline parameters. Overlay menu input does not trigger game button conditions.

examples.title: Run three lines while holding L + R
examples.text: Run the next three lines when the button condition matches; otherwise skip the controlled lines.

sections.title: Memory comparisons
intro: Read a value and compare it with the supplied value to decide whether the next AA lines run. X selects both the relation and the width, giving 12 combinations.
fields: Select a combination from the table below.
The hexadecimal number of following controlled lines.
A hexadecimal value or bit pattern of the selected width.
notes: Z06 / Overlay compare raw values at the selected width. Greater-than and less-than comparisons are unsigned integer comparisons, not floating-point arithmetic.
A failed condition skips its controlled range; unrelated following codes may still run. Nested counts must respect physical lines and multiline instruction boundaries.

examples.title: Write when a byte equals 5
examples.text: If the 8-bit value at `81504000` equals 5, write decimal 999,999,999 as 32 bits at `81504780`. The write opcode corrects a typo in the original PDF.

sections.title: Version differences and errata
intro: This guide covers the original PDF's file structure, line layout, and all nine code families, plus the Z06 B2 update. Page references use the printed manual numbering; the PDF page index is one greater.
fields: ANSI belongs to Z04. The Z06 site specifies UTF-8; Overlay supports UTF-8 / GBK.
Original `_V1` starts ON. New Overlay sessions start with every entry OFF.
The PDF mentions 50 descriptions / 200 lines. The Z06 site specifies 50 groups with up to 200 lines each. Overlay uses separate limits.
The module index is XX; the second field's Y selects the segment. Do not exchange them.
The manual requires equal chain depths and widths; this alone does not define later implementations.
Keep the old mode table as a reference. Z06 / Overlay match the complete button mask.
notes: The text-segment examples mix numeric bit patterns with byte order. This guide uses little-endian interpretation: `BF00` produces bytes `00 BF`; the value is not reversed again.
The condition example's `$2000` conflicts with the direct-write format. It is explicitly corrected to `$0200` here.
The third compressed-pointer example has a base-address mismatch in its comment. This guide follows `82E40F10` in the code rather than the stale comment.
This is a format reference. Older firmware requirements, group limits, or search features are not applied to VitaCheat Overlay.
